name: command-processor
intent: Separate the request for a service from its execution: every request is reified as a command object that a dedicated processor queues, schedules and executes, so callers never name a receiver or a thread while the processor adds logging, undo, macro grouping, prioritisation and replay on top of that single seam.
problem: When requests are handled inline, three decisions are welded together in the request handler: who performs the work, when and on which thread it runs, and what is recorded about it afterwards. As operations multiply, the handler degenerates into a growing switch over request types that every new command or altered argument forces someone to edit - and adding undo, a history, macro recording, deferred or prioritised execution, or replay after a crash then means editing every call site instead of one component.
context: Interactive, batch or server-side systems whose requests must be queued, scheduled, recorded or replayed rather than executed inline: GUI action histories with undo/redo and macros, CQRS-style application layers, job/device controllers, and workflow engines. It pays off once at least one added service (logging, undo, macro/transaction, deferred or prioritised execution, distribution across workers) is genuinely required; for immediate synchronous requests the same indirection is pure overhead.
benefits: Invocation is decoupled from execution: the client constructs a command and never names the receiver, the thread that runs it, or the moment it runs.

Because requests are first-class objects, cross-cutting services become possible at all - execution log, undo/redo, macro recording, replay, prioritisation, rate limiting and retry live in the processor instead of being duplicated at each call site.
Several requests can be grouped into one transaction or macro, giving all-or-nothing semantics over a sequence of operations.
New command types are added by registering a handler/receiver variant; the processor, the queue and existing commands stay untouched.
Deferred, batched or distributed execution comes for free: the same command object can be executed by an in-process worker, persisted and executed later, or shipped to another node.
Testability: commands are values, so they can be constructed, queued, asserted and replayed in tests while the processor runs against a fake repository and a synchronous executor.
tradeoffs: Every request pays an extra hop (client -> repository -> processor -> receiver) plus dynamic dispatch, so latency and code volume grow even for trivial operations.

The queue is a new single point of failure and a new single point of serialisation: unbounded, it converts overload into memory pressure and eventually OOM instead of backpressure; bounded without a rejection policy it converts overload into dropped or blocking producers.

Losing the synchronous return path makes failures asynchronous: unless results and errors are recorded per command, a failing command vanishes silently, and duplicate execution (retry, replay, at-least-once transport) is possible unless commands carry idempotency keys.
Undo only works while every command is genuinely invertible and the inverse order is preserved per scope; commands that mutate shared state out of band or perform I/O cannot be undone reliably.
The execution log holds domain data, so it duplicates state, needs its own retention/redaction rules, and is easily confused with the domain event log - replaying it can re-trigger effects.
Debugging and reasoning span four components (client, repository, processor, receiver), and the command abstraction itself adds a concept every new developer must learn.

participants.responsibility: Turns a user, protocol or batch request into a concrete command object and hands it to the processor; it never names the receiver or decides when the work runs.
Uniform interface of all commands: execute the request (and, where undo is promised, a matching inverse). Commands are interchangeable to the processor.
Encapsulates one request: the parameters, the receiver it acts on, and any state needed to execute, log and undo it. Should be a serialisable value whenever replay or persistence is claimed.
Abstract processor: accepts commands from the client, defines the policy surface (execution, storage, history, undo) and hides how and where commands are executed.
Implements the policy: places commands in the repository, allocates threads or an event loop, applies priority/delay, appends executed commands to the history and drives macros/transactions.
Holds commands that are waiting, deferred or already executed; backs inspection, replay and undo. Bounded by design, with an explicit overflow policy.
Performs the actual application work for a command; knows nothing about queueing, logging or undo.

use_cases: Interactive applications where every user action is a command, so undo/redo, macro recording and scripted playback are uniform (editors, CAD, IDEs, drawing tools).
CQRS application layers: HTTP or message-handler endpoints validate a command, dispatch it to one handler, and the processor adds logging, retries, correlation and audit.
Batch and offline job processing: commands are persisted with their parameters, executed later by a worker pool, and replayed from the log after a crash.
Device and machine control: hardware operations are queued, sequenced with priorities and delays, and replayed after a restart while the physical receiver stays out of the client's reach.
Multi-step business transactions and sagas: a macro/transaction command groups several commands and the processor guarantees their ordering, compensation or rollback.
Simulation and game loops: input is translated into commands that a scheduler executes at the right tick, decoupling input handling from simulation state.

Workflow engines and long-running processes: multi-step business workflows (hotel checkouts, code review approvals, customer onboarding) where each step is a command/steps are coordinated by a process manager with durable execution across process restarts.

Distributed systems with compensating transactions: operations like ReserveInventory / ReleaseInventory, where each step is a command that can be individually retried, compensated, or replayed from an event store.

Offline-first optimistic UI: client-side commands are executed immediately against local state, queued in a pending/outbox, and reconciled with the server when connectivity resumes (e.g., Replicache, local-first databases).

Internal iterators and callbacks in languages lacking closures: commands replace callbacks in Java Swing, SWT, and other GUI frameworks, enabling parameterised actions to be queued, logged, or undone.

Transactional outbox patterns: database changes are queued as commands within the same transaction, then published reliably by a background worker, ensuring at-least-once delivery without distributed transactions.
Actor-based systems (Akka, Orleans): commands are the primary message type between actors, with the mailbox acting as the command repository and the actor's behavior as the processor.
Event sourcing systems: commands are validated and produce events; the command processor validates command preconditions, the event store records the resulting state changes, enabling full replay.
GraphQL mutation pipelines: each mutation is a command that passes through a processor for validation, authorization, audit logging, and eventual execution against the domain model.
Blockchain/smart contract operations: operations are encapsulated as commands with built-in compensation, sequenced and replayed to reconstruct state from genesis.
GNU Emacs: the command loop reads key sequences, resolves them to interactive command objects, and executes them via command-execute, backing keyboard macros, command history and undo boundaries.

Cocoa/Cocoa Touch apps: NSUndoManager acts as the command processor - every state-changing operation registers its inverse, and beginUndoGrouping/endUndoGrouping bundle related operations into one undoable group.
Java Swing/AWT: AbstractAction plus ActionMap/InputMap dispatch user gestures through command objects that the framework queues and maps to key bindings and menu items.
avoid_when: A single synchronous call with no queueing, logging or undo requirement: a direct method call (or the plain Command pattern) is simpler and clearer.
The need is exactly-once delivery across processes: use a messaging broker with the delivery guarantees and transactional client of the messaging layer instead of hand-rolling durability.
Requests are trivial, fire-and-forget and idempotent: a plain worker pool, thread pool or event loop with no processor layer conveys the same behaviour with less ceremony.
Behaviour varies with one object's internal state rather than with queued requests: State expresses that directly.
The platform already owns the dispatch loop and the application has no history/undo requirement: configure the existing executor or request queue instead of re-implementing a processor over it.

related_patterns_notes.command: The foundational GoF pattern; Command Processor extends Command by adding a dedicated processor component that manages execution policy, queuing, history and orthogonal services (undo, logging, retry). Where Command focuses on request encapsulation, Command Processor focuses on request management.
related_patterns_notes.saga: A saga uses compensating commands to handle distributed transactions; Command Processor is the execution substrate that runs each step. The saga orchestrator directs a sequence of commands, while the command processor handles the mechanics of execution, retry and logging.
related_patterns_notes.process-manager: Both coordinate multi-step workflows; the process manager holds the workflow state machine and issues commands, while the command processor executes those commands and handles the mechanics (queuing, retry, logging).
related_patterns_notes.event-sourcing: Event sourcing stores state changes as an immutable event log; Command Processor sits upstream validating commands that produce events. Commands are the write side; events are the persisted record. Replay in event sourcing replays events, not commands. event-sourcing
related_patterns_notes.cqrs: CQRS separates command and query paths; Command Processor is the infrastructure for the command side, validating and executing commands while the query side materialises read models from events. cqrs
related_patterns_notes.memento: Memento captures state snapshots for undo; Command Processor can use mementos as the undo mechanism for commands that store before-state. They address different aspects of reversibility.
related_patterns_notes.active-object: Active Object decouples method invocation from execution on its own thread; Command Processor is the more general pattern that adds queuing, history and cross-cutting concerns beyond just thread decoupling.
related_patterns_notes.interceptor: Interceptor lets framework code invoke callbacks around command execution; Command Processor can use interceptors to layer cross-cutting concerns (logging, metrics, tracing) without coupling to the processor itself.
related_patterns_notes.thread-pool: Thread Pool provides worker threads for executing tasks; Command Processor uses a thread pool as an execution strategy for running commands concurrently.
related_patterns_notes.futures: Futures represent asynchronous results; Command Processor can return futures for commands that need to report results back to the caller after async execution.

anti_patterns: Command buses whose command objects are thin wrappers around a service lookup, with no queueing, logging, undo or scheduling to show for the extra indirection ('command soup').
An unbounded in-memory queue declared to be the reliability layer: throughput is fine until the producer outruns the workers, after which the process dies of memory exhaustion.
Treating the execution log as an audit or event log without the accompanying idempotency, ordering and retention rules, so replay duplicates effects and the log leaks payload data.
Advertising undo while allowing commands that are not invertible, that perform I/O, or that mutate shared state behind the processor's back.
Fire-and-forget dispatch with no result store: failures disappear, and every caller ends up re-implementing its own retry and timeout logic.
Command class explosion: creating a distinct command class for every operation when a parameterized command or record would suffice, inflating the codebase without proportional benefit.
Hidden receivers: commands that pull dependencies from globals or service locators instead of receiving them explicitly, making the command's inputs opaque and hard to test or replay.

Stale undo: executing an undo operation on state that has changed since the original command ran (e.g., a text editor undo that restores a deleted line that has since been modified by another user), producing counter-intuitive results.
Unsafe retries without idempotency: retrying a non-idempotent command (e.g., charging a credit card, sending an email) on a transient failure, causing the side effect to repeat.
Mutable shared commands: sharing a stateful undo-capable command instance across threads or multiple undo-history entries, causing cross-contamination of undo state.
Command-object explosion in long-running editors: storing every keystroke as a separate command in the undo stack without coalescing or bounding, leading to memory bloat in long sessions.
Confusing commands with events: treating commands (intentions to change state) as events (facts that have happened), causing replay to re-trigger side effects and breaking audit accuracy.
Anti-commands with non-sequential undo: using anti-commands (inverse operations like x-- for x++) that can be undone out of order, leading to inconsistent state in multi-step workflows.
Monolithic command processor: packing hundreds of unrelated doWorkN methods into a single processor class, violating single responsibility and making the class an unmaintainable 'god object'.

Blocking the processor thread: executing slow or blocking operations (synchronous I/O, external API calls) inside the command processor loop, starving queued commands and defeating the purpose of async execution.
Schema drift: command payload schema evolving independently from handler validation, causing silent failures or data corruption when older command versions are replayed.

Memory bloat from large object capture: commands holding references to entire object graphs (e.g., the whole document) instead of just the minimum delta (e.g., the changed range), causing heap exhaustion in long sessions.
Downcasting and type-checking: needing instanceof or downcasting in the processor indicates a too-coarse command interface that has become a maintenance burden.
Silent failure swallowing: catching exceptions and returning 'Accepted' without durable execution, leaving callers believing the operation succeeded when it failed.
Priority queue starvation: low-priority commands never drained because high-priority commands continuously arrive, violating fairness guarantees.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: formulating a request, deciding when it runs, and performing it live in three different components.
Reification: a request becomes a first-class value, which is what makes logging, undo, replay and grouping expressible at all.
Inversion of control (Hollywood principle): the processor calls the command; commands never drive the scheduler.
Open/closed principle: new requests arrive as new command/handler registrations, not as edits to the processor.
Information hiding: the scheduling, threading and history policy is hidden behind the processor interface.
Liskov substitution: all concrete commands must be interchangeable through the command interface, otherwise the processor needs type tests.
Single responsibility: the command processor should only manage execution policy; domain logic belongs in receivers/handlers, not in the processor itself.
Interface segregation: prefer small, focused command interfaces (execute + optional undo) over fat interfaces with many lifecycle methods.
best_practices: Keep commands immutable value objects carrying data plus a receiver/handler reference; resolve dependencies inside the handler, not through a service locator in the command.
Bound the repository and choose an explicit overflow policy (block, reject, spill to disk, shed load); never let an unbounded queue stand in for backpressure.
Give every command an identity (command id or dedupe key) and make handlers idempotent so retries, replay and at-least-once transports cannot duplicate effects.
Keep the execution history separate from the domain event/audit log, with its own retention, redaction and replay rules.
Run the shortest possible critical section inside the processor: dequeue under the lock, execute outside it, and never hold the repository lock across a command boundary.
Use the platform's executor/queue primitives instead of hand-rolled thread-plus-sleep loops, and make the scheduling policy explicit (ordered, pooled, prioritised, delayed).
Only promise undo for commands with a genuine inverse, and keep undo/redo stacks scoped (per session, per document, per macro) so inverse order is preserved.

Design self-describing commands: each command should carry metadata (name, timestamp, affected entities, preconditions/postconditions) so undo/redo operations are transparent, debuggable, and auditable.

For distributed or concurrent undo/redo, enforce strict chronological ordering: use a centralized, thread-safe command stack and validate application state after every undo/redo operation with invariant checks.

Use versioned commands with expectedVersion (optimistic concurrency control) when multiple actors can submit commands concurrently against the same aggregate; detect CAS mismatches and treat them as semantic conflicts.

Prefer compensating commands over true inversion for distributed systems: rather than rolling back a single transaction, emit a ReleaseInventory command to undo a ReserveInventory, making the intent explicit and auditable.

Implement command self-configuration (Zarras): let concrete commands self-configure with required data and receiver at execution time via an Informant object, rather than letting the invoker or client become coupled to concrete command class details.

Manage memory for long-running undo histories: capture the minimum state needed for inversion (e.g., old value, position) rather than full snapshots; consider periodic checkpoints or coalescing successive commands.
Distinguish failure types: transient infrastructure failures merit bounded retry with exponential backoff; semantic conflicts (version mismatch) should return to the client for manual reconciliation.
Use async/await at processor boundaries rather than blocking on futures inside the core loop; keep the executor free for other commands.
Instrument the command processor with metrics: queue depth, execution latency, error rates and retry counts per command type to detect degradation before it becomes an outage.
Version command schemas explicitly and validate at ingestion; reject or transform commands with outdated schemas rather than letting schema drift cause silent failures.
Design command handlers to be idempotent and stateless; any state needed for execution should come from the command payload or a snapshot, not from in-memory state that survives command completion.
For high-throughput systems, consider command coalescing: merge successive commands of the same type (e.g., multiple keystrokes) into a single undoable unit to bound memory while preserving intent.
Capture only the minimum delta needed for undo (e.g., the removed text, not the whole document) to prevent memory bloat in long-running undo histories.

Ensure all command payloads and their transitive dependencies are fully serializable when persistence, network transmission, or distributed execution is required; non-serializable receiver references break replay and audit.

Design command timeout and cancellation policies explicitly; a command that times out should leave the system in a known state (committed, rolled back, or rescheduled) rather than an indeterminate condition.
Use a circuit breaker around the command processor's downstream dependencies to prevent cascading failures from overwhelming the queue when back-end services degrade.

Prefer a single-threaded command loop for commands requiring strict ordering, and a thread pool only when commands are independent and order does not matter; mixing both in one processor creates subtle race conditions.

(Addison-Wesley; 1996; book) — The canonical Command Processor pattern description. Defines the pattern as separating the request for a service from its execution via command objects, a command processor, and suppliers. Chapter 20 covers the pattern in the context of a pattern language for concurrent and networked objects.
https://www.amazon.com/Pattern-Oriented-Software-Architecture-Patterns-Concurrent-Networked/dp/0471958697

Peter Sommerlad. Pattern Languages of Program Design 2. (Addison-Wesley; 1996; book-chapter; 63-74) — ORIGINAL PUBLICATION of the Command Processor pattern before its inclusion in POSA. Describes separating request encoding from execution, scheduling, logging, and undo support in a pattern language context.
https://dl.acm.org/doi/book/10.5555/525302

Peter Sommerlad. Command Processor. (HSR.ch / Pattern Tracking; 2014; pattern-article) — Pattern prototype at HSR pattern tracking site. Confirms Command Processor separates request for a service from its execution; manages requests as objects, schedules execution, stores for undo.
https://wiki.hsr.ch/APF/files/CommandProcessor.pdf

Roger Whitney. CS635 Advanced OOAD: Functor, Command, Command Processor. (San Diego State University; 1998; course-notes) — References POSA as primary Command Processor source (Buschmann et al. 1996, pp. 277-290) and Sommerlad 1996 PLoP paper (pp. 63-74). Confirms Command Processor is a distinct pattern from GoF Command.
https://eli.sdsu.edu/courses/spring98/cs635/notes/command/command.html

Thomas Minka. Command Pattern. (MIT; 2005; academic-notes) — Explicitly describes Command Processor as an entity that queues, prioritizes, and distributes Commands. Discusses logging, undo via replay/checkpoint, and scheduling. Extends GoF Command with lifecycle management.
https://alumni.media.mit.edu/~tpminka/patterns/Command.html

Douglas C. Schmidt. Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects (POSA2). (Vanderbilt University; 2000; book) — Companion volume to POSA1, covering patterns for concurrency and networking. Command Processor appears within the broader pattern language for concurrent and networked objects.
https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/POSA/

Gregor Hohpe, Bobby Woolf. Enterprise Integration Patterns. (Addison-Wesley; 2003; book) — Describes Command Message pattern and messaging-based request handling. 65 integration patterns used in enterprise messaging systems, directly relevant to distributed command processing.
https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/

Martin Fowler. Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (PoEAA). (Addison-Wesley; 2003; book) — Catalog includes Command pattern as a domain logic pattern. Fowler's catalog is the authoritative enterprise architecture reference for command-query separation and related patterns.
https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/

Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, John Vlissides. Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (GoF). (Addison-Wesley; 1995; book; 233-242) — Command pattern (GoF) is the FOUNDATION that Command Processor extends. Command Processor ADDS management, scheduling, undo, and logging to Command objects - these are distinct patterns.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_Patterns

Paramore/Brighter Documentation. Command, Processor and Dispatcher Patterns. (GitBook; 2026; framework-docs) — Modern .NET framework documentation clearly distinguishing Command (encapsulates request), Command Dispatcher (links request to handler), and Command Processor (schedules/executes with orthogonal concerns like logging/retry/undo).
https://brightercommand.gitbook.io/paramore-brighter-documentation/understanding-brighter/commandscommanddispatcherandprocessor

Robert H. B. and contributors. Design Patterns In Action - Command Pattern. (2026; pattern-article) — Surveys macro commands, optimistic commands (offline-first with pending queue), command coalescing (burst-merging for keystroke efficiency), and discusses stale undo when external state changes between execute and undo.
https://designpatternsinaction.com/pattern/command/

Software Patterns Lexicon - Command Pattern for Java. (2026; pattern-article) — Comprehensive guide covering command vs Runnable/Callable/lambdas, undo mechanisms (inverse ops, snapshots, compensating commands), thread-safety rules, retry/idempotency, cancellation/timeouts, and detailed pitfalls section.
https://softwarepatternslexicon.com/java/behavioral-patterns/command-pattern/

Robert Nystrom. Command Pattern - Game Programming Patterns. (2026; book) — Bob Nystrom's free online book (worked on at Electronic Arts) explains Command pattern with emphasis on undo/redo, macro commands, and input handling in game loops. Practical, well-illustrated treatment.
https://gameprogrammingpatterns.com/command.html

Refactoring Guru. Command Pattern - Refactoring Guru. (2026; pattern-article) — Comprehensive command pattern coverage with UML diagrams, implementation guidance, comparison to alternatives, and relationship to other patterns. One of the most widely referenced online pattern resources.
https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/command

Oskar Dudycz. Saga and Process Manager - distributed processes in practice. (Event-Driven.io; 2023; article) — Clarifies distinction between Saga (choreography-based compensation) and Process Manager (orchestrated workflow state machine), both consuming commands from a command processor.
https://event-driven.io/en/saga_process_manager_distributed_transactions/

Chris Richardson. Pattern: Saga. (Microservices.io; 2026; pattern-article) — Practical implementation guide for saga pattern in microservices using choreography or orchestration, with command-based coordination and compensating transactions.
https://microservices.io/patterns/data/saga.html

Temporal Labs. Temporal Documentation - Durable Execution. (2026; framework-docs) — Temporal provides durable execution - workflows that survive process crashes. Activities are processed as commands with automatic retry, timeout, and heartbeat. Task queues act as command repositories. Used in production by NVIDIA, Salesforce, Snap, OpenAI.
https://temporal.io

AxonIQ. Axon Framework - CQRS and Event Sourcing. (2026; framework-docs) — Production Java framework implementing CQRS and event sourcing. Command handlers receive commands and produce events; the framework manages command routing, validation, and event emission.
https://docs.axoniq.io

Microsoft. CQRS Pattern - Azure Architecture Center. (2025; architecture-guide) — Microsoft's authoritative guide on CQRS pattern separating commands from queries, with Command Processor as the infrastructure for the command (write) side.
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cqrs

Microsoft. Saga Pattern - Azure Architecture Center. (2025; architecture-guide) — Covers orchestration vs choreography approaches to multi-service transactions using compensating commands, relevant to command processor implementations in distributed systems.
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga

Martin Fowler. Event Sourcing - Martin Fowler. (2025; article) — Fowler's authoritative article on event sourcing. Commands are validated and produce events; the command processor validates command preconditions. Replay in event sourcing replays events, not commands.
https://martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-sourcing.html

Vanderbilt University / Douglas Schmidt. Command Processor - POSA Pattern Summary. (2006; academic-notes) — Summary PDF of the POSA Command Processor pattern with implementation hints, relationship to other patterns, and practical usage notes from the Schmidt research group.
https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/PDF/CommandProcessor.pdf

Benoit Dupire, Eduardo B. Fernandez. The Command Dispatcher Pattern. (2001; conference-paper) — PLoP 2001 paper proposing Command Dispatcher as a runtime-extensible pattern where handlers are registered by name, enabling addition/removal of commands without recompilation.

(University of Ioannina; 1996; conference-paper) — Identifies five anti-patterns arising when command configuration responsibility is misplaced: Invoker-configured commands, factory-configured commands, and others. Introduces Command Self-Configuration pattern.
https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.50.9292

AxonIQ. Command Dispatchers - Axon Framework Reference. (2026; framework-docs) — Official Axon Framework docs: the CommandBus dispatches each CommandMessage to exactly one handler, dispatch is async via CompletableFuture, and CommandGateway/CommandDispatcher are the client seams - a production implementation of the POSA Command Processor with correlation data and a Unit of Work processing context.
https://docs.axoniq.io/axon-framework-reference/development/commands/command-dispatchers/

Apple. Undo Architecture: Undo Manager. (2026; framework-docs) — Apple's official docs for NSUndoManager: reversible operations are registered with target/selector or NSInvocation, grouped per user action via beginUndoGrouping/endUndoGrouping, stacked for undo/redo, and cappable with setLevelsOfUndo: - the command processor and history in a shipping GUI framework.
https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/Cocoa/Conceptual/UndoArchitecture/Articles/UndoManager.html

(2026; official-manual) — The Emacs command loop reads key sequences, translates them to interactive commands and executes them via command-execute/call-interactively; the interactive form is command self-configuration, and keyboard macros plus command history are processor-level services in a decades-deployed editor.
https://www.math.utah.edu/docs/info/elisp_19.html

(Medium; 2025; article) — Criticism of blanket command-bus adoption: classifying every operation as a command/query adds mental models, pipeline middleware cost and diagnostic burden without scaling pressure; 'overuse driven by clean-architecture perception' sacrifices clarity for ceremony.
https://medium.com/@kerimkkara/cqrs-in-net-the-decision-youll-regret-if-you-scale-too-early-b00d2374525c

(DEV Community; 2026; article) — Misuse critique: defaulting to a mediator/command bus turns a single operation into command + handler + registration plumbing in typical CRUD apps; adds indirection without delivering the queueing/undo/scheduling services that justify a command processor.
